subject: physics
title: Particle model and pressure
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Particle model and pressure — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.3.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Particle model and pressure, specification section 4.3.3.
final_note: You worked through Particle model and pressure — 16 specification statements.

concepts.def: The molecules of a gas are in constant random motion. They travel in all directions and at a wide range of speeds, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of the container. No molecule keeps one path or one speed for long.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules. Raising the temperature raises that average, so the molecules move faster on average. Individual molecules still have a range of speeds; temperature describes the average, not any one molecule.

Gas pressure arises from the collisions of the moving gas molecules with the walls of the container. Each collision exerts a small force on the wall; the huge number of collisions every second adds up to a steady net force spread over the wall area.

A gas is at constant volume when it is sealed in a rigid container that cannot expand or contract, so the space the gas occupies cannot change. Only the temperature and the pressure are free to change.

concepts.term: Pressure and temperature at constant volume
concepts.def: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure it exerts. Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so the molecules hit the walls more frequently and with more force, and the pressure rises. Cooling has the opposite effect.

concepts.term: Net force at right angles to a surface
concepts.def: The pressure of a gas produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or to any surface in contact with the gas. Molecules arrive from every direction, so the sideways parts of their impacts cancel out and only the component perpendicular to the surface remains.

concepts.term: Compression and expansion of a gas
concepts.def: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes. Unlike a solid or a liquid, the molecules of a gas are far apart, so the volume the gas occupies can be squeezed down or allowed to grow when the pressure acting on it changes.

If a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature is given a larger volume, the molecules keep the same average kinetic energy but are spread through a bigger space. Each molecule travels further between wall collisions, so fewer collisions happen each second on each square metre of wall, and the pressure falls.

concepts.term: Fixed mass of gas at constant temperature
concepts.def: The condition under which pressure × volume = constant holds. The same molecules must stay sealed in the container, with none added or lost, and the temperature must not change. If gas escapes or the temperature changes, the relationship no longer applies.

For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]. Pressure and volume change in opposite directions: doubling the pressure halves the volume, and tripling the volume divides the pressure by three.

The unit of pressure. In the relationship p V = constant the pressure, p, is in pascals, Pa. One pascal is one newton per square metre, so a pressure is a force spread over an area, not a force on its own.

The unit of volume used in this relationship: volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3. Volumes quoted in cubic centimetres or in litres must be converted to m^3 before they are used alongside pressures in pascals.

concepts.term: Using p V = constant in a calculation
concepts.def: Because p V has the same value before and after the change, the initial pressure × the initial volume equals the final pressure × the final volume. Multiply the two quantities you know together, then divide by the third to find the missing pressure or the missing volume.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force. When a force moves something, energy is transferred from one store to another, and the amount of energy transferred is the work done.

The energy stored by the molecules of a gas, made up of the kinetic energy of their motion and the potential energy of their positions. Doing work on a gas increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause an increase in the temperature of the gas.

concepts.term: Doing work on an enclosed gas
concepts.def: When a force pushes a piston into a sealed gas, the piston moves while pushing on the gas, so work is done on the gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas, which can raise its temperature — this is why the barrel of a bicycle pump becomes warm in use.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the molecules of a gas is correct?
options: They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to their average kinetic energy.
They are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is set by their total kinetic energy.
They all move at one single fixed speed, and the temperature of the gas is set by that shared speed.
They move along fixed repeating paths, and the temperature of the gas is set by their spacing.
mcqs.explain: This is what the specification states: the molecules of a gas are in constant random motion, and the temperature of the gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the molecules.

mcqs.q: A sealed container of gas is heated and the temperature of the gas rises. What happens to the molecules of the gas?
options: They all speed up by exactly the same amount and keep sharing one common speed.
Their average kinetic energy rises, so the molecules move faster on average.
Each molecule expands, so the gas now fills more of the container space.
They collide with one another less often, now that they have energy.
mcqs.explain: The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so raising the temperature raises that average and the molecules move faster on average.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas is sealed in a rigid container, so its volume cannot change. The gas is then heated. What happens to the pressure the gas exerts?
options: It stays the same, because the trapped gas is not able to expand.
It falls, because the heated molecules swell and spread apart.
It increases, because the molecules hit the walls harder.
It rises briefly, then falls back to its old value.
mcqs.explain: Changing the temperature of a gas held at constant volume changes the pressure exerted: the faster molecules strike the walls more often and with greater force.

mcqs.q: What causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
options: The gas molecules repelling each other and pushing on the walls.
The weight of the gas above pressing down on the container.
The molecules swelling up and pressing against the walls.
The molecules of the gas colliding with the walls of it.
mcqs.explain: Gas pressure comes from the huge number of collisions the randomly moving molecules make with the walls each second, each collision exerting a small force.

mcqs.q: Two identical rigid sealed flasks hold the same gas. Flask X is kept at 20 °C and flask Y at 80 °C. Why is the pressure in flask Y higher?
options: The molecules in Y have swollen to a larger size, so they press harder on the walls.
The molecules in Y have a greater average kinetic energy, so they hit the walls harder.
The molecules in Y repel one another far more strongly at the higher temperature.
The molecules in Y are packed more closely together than those in flask X.
mcqs.explain: The higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so in the same fixed volume the collisions with the walls are both more frequent and more forceful.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas is cooled while its volume is kept constant. Using the particle model, what happens to the pressure of the gas?
options: It stays the same, because the rigid container will not let the gas shrink at all.
It increases, because the cooled molecules move closer to the walls of it.
It decreases, because slower molecules hit the walls less often and less hard.
It decreases, because the molecules shrink in size as the gas cools down.
mcqs.explain: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy, so the molecules collide with the walls both less frequently and with less force, and the pressure falls.

mcqs.q: The pressure of a gas produces a net force on the wall of its container. In which direction does that net force act?
options: At an angle that depends on the shape of the container.
Along the surface of the wall, in the direction of flow.
Straight down, because of the weight of the gas.
At right angles to the surface of the container wall.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the pressure produces a net force at right angles to the wall of the gas container, or any surface, because the sideways parts of the impacts cancel.

mcqs.q: Which statement about a gas and changes of pressure is correct?
options: A gas can be compressed or expanded by pressure changes.
A gas keeps a fixed volume whatever pressure is applied to it.
A gas can be expanded by pressure changes but never compressed.
A gas can only be compressed if it is squeezed from above.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: the molecules of a gas are far apart, so a change of pressure can squeeze the gas into a smaller volume or let it expand.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas is allowed to expand into a larger volume at constant temperature. Using the particle model, why does the pressure decrease?
options: Each molecule strikes the wall more gently, since it now has less kinetic energy.
The molecules cool down as they spread out into the much larger space.
The molecules travel further between wall collisions, so there are fewer collisions.
The molecules shrink in size once they are given more room to move about.
mcqs.explain: At constant temperature the molecules keep the same average speed, but in a larger volume each one takes longer to reach a wall, so the collision rate and the pressure both fall.

mcqs.q: Under which conditions does the relationship pressure × volume = constant apply to a gas?
options: Any mass of gas at all, whatever its temperature happens to be doing.
A fixed mass of gas whose temperature is steadily climbing.
Any gas at all, so long as its container has been sealed.
A fixed mass of gas that is being held at a constant temperature.
mcqs.explain: The specification introduces the relationship with exactly this condition: for a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant.

mcqs.q: For a fixed mass of gas held at a constant temperature, which relationship does the specification give?
options: pressure × volume = constant, written as [p V = constant]
pressure ÷ volume = constant, written as [p / V = a constant]
pressure + volume = constant, written as [p + V = constant]
pressure × volume = temperature, written as [p V = T]
mcqs.explain: This is the relationship exactly as the specification states it, together with the symbol form the specification gives in brackets.

mcqs.q: Which units does the specification give for the two quantities in p V = constant?
options: Pressure in newtons, N, and volume in centimetres cubed, cm^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres cubed, m^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in cubic centimetres, cm^3.
Pressure in pascals, Pa, and volume in metres squared, m^2.
mcqs.explain: The specification states pressure, p, in pascals, Pa, and volume, V, in metres cubed, m^3.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 0.125 m^3 at a pressure of 80 kPa. At constant temperature the pressure is increased to 800 kPa. What is the new volume of the gas?
mcqs.explain: p V = constant, so 80 × 0.125 = 800 × V, giving V = 10 ÷ 800 = 0.0125 m^3. The pressure is ten times larger, so the volume is ten times smaller.

mcqs.q: A fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 300 kPa occupies 0.020 m^3. At constant temperature it is allowed to expand to 0.150 m^3. What is the new pressure of the gas?
options: 40 kPa
300 kPa
2250 kPa
mcqs.explain: p V = constant, so 300 × 0.020 = p × 0.150, giving p = 6.0 ÷ 0.150 = 40 kPa. The gas has expanded, so the pressure must fall.

mcqs.q: In physics, what is meant by work?
options: Work is the energy stored inside a moving body.
Work is the transfer of energy by a force.
Work is a force acting over a given distance.
Work is the heating caused by a force.
mcqs.explain: This is the specification statement: work is the transfer of energy by a force.

mcqs.q: A cyclist uses a bicycle pump to inflate a tyre, and the barrel of the pump becomes noticeably warm. Which explanation is correct?
options: Friction between the piston seal and the barrel is the only cause of the warming.
Warm air is drawn in from outside, and that air heats the metal barrel.
Work is done on the gas as it is compressed, raising its internal energy.
The gas loses internal energy as it is squeezed, so heat is released.
mcqs.explain: The piston exerts a force that moves, so work is done on the enclosed gas. That transfer increases the internal energy of the gas and can cause its temperature to rise.
